Reconstructing the economy

By: Siniketiwe Hlanze | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Following the worst economic decline in centuries due to the pandemic, what will it take resuscitate South Africa’s economy.

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa’s has seen its economy steadily decline over the past decade, registering a less than one percent growth before the pandemic, it stood no fight chance once COVID 19 hit our shores.

Already downgraded to sub-investment grade by all three major ratings agencies, job losses and a contracted GDP due to lockdown, a strong recovery plan became imperative. President Cyril Ramaphosa’s recovery plan has focused on industry as the main driving force to get South Africa back on a growth path. This means manufacturing and infrastructure development are some of the sectors that will be getting both policy and financial support from government with the expectation of more jobs and revenue. The insert will trace South Africa's recovery plan thus far and analyze the possible growth trajectory of manufacturing and infrastructure as economic boosters.



Summary:
President Cyril Ramaphosa inherited a country facing serious economic woes, over the years he has devised various efforts to rekindle economic growth, his annual investment summits, various advisory groups etc. It is imperative especially after the devastation of the pandemic that the heavy lifting to fix the economy must start.

One of the interventions outlined by the president in October last year was to 'unlock more than R1 trillion in infrastructure investment over the next four years'. In his budget speech, Finance Minister Tito Mboweni promised an injection of R700 billion into infrastructure development as a means to kick start the economy, both highlighting infrastructure as a cornerstone for the recovery of the economy.
Another important focus of the economic reconstruction plan is to revitalise manufacturing in the country, in 1994 manufacturing accounted for 20 percent of the GDP and this has declined to 14 percent currently. Both these sectors are labour intensive and offer long term investment opportunities. However South Africa has a history of being lackadaisical when it comes to implementation of policy and creating plans on top of more plans. Due to the state of the economy, the implementation of this reconstruction plan is urgent for the country.

Script:


Scenes of looting, destruction of retail stores, the burning of major warehouses and trucks and damaged to infrastructure in KwaZulu Natal and parts of Gauteng sent shock waves across the country and rattled our economy, which is teetering on a path of tentative recovery.

With damage estimated to be in the billions and thousands of jobs lost, rebuilding the economy and a wrecked country, puts President Cyril Ramaphosa’s recovery and reconstruction in plan in the spotlight.

Announced in October last year, it promised to build roads, maintain municipal infrastructure and revive sectors like construction and manufacturing.
Fixing the basics.
An interrupted water and power supply means factories can operate optimally, better roads allows for easier transportation of goods and maintained infrastructure makes running businesses like retail stores run efficiently.
A vital link in any supply chain is functioning infrastructure as any interruptions can trigger huge losses,

Potholes, consistent water shortages and black outs in Lichtenburg, in the North West province are driving out a major Clover cheese factory.

The dairy company contends that numerous efforts to engage the local municipality on these matters have been futile.
For economist Gina Schoeman, the president’s plan will be important to saving local jobs.



















Masa [ CLIP 2, 00;33]
the idea of our economy being centred around infrastructure is not entirely new, as great as it is, we’ve heard of it during the mbeki era, what’s different this time around, because it seems that it’s something quite big in this plan
Gina 01;07 – Infrastructure has deteriorated, maintenance of infrastructure has deteriorated, to such a large degree now that on a municipal and provincial level the type of lack of service delivery you’re seeing is becoming a huge dissentive for companies to invest more or for companies to stick around, so the need for infrastructure has never been greater.
Astral Foods in Standerton, Mpumalanga, says it has lost millions of rands at its processing factory, in the town drowning in sewage, with an irregular water supply.
WALKING LINK; Reginiting infrastructure development can boost other sectors, especially labour intensive industries with mass hiring potential
Denver
But the pandemic brought a different element completely, it was very difficult, as an insider when I saw those in coming order numbers, those volumes were so low it was frightening and it’s a simple case of economics., supply and demand and the reality is the demand side has completely dropped, there was nothing coming from industry really even the end consumer was not spending quite as much so it did affect the industry in quite a bad way.
Denver Berman Jacob is executive director at Sweet-Orr, he has been in the textile industry for decades. He’s seen, first hand, the decline of the industry but it was the pandemic that almost left this once thriving trade hanging by a thread.
Denver 05:58 sweet-orr is representative of the industry at large, no we are not back to pre-pandemic levels and we don’t think we will be for the next 2 years. This is gonna take time to get out of the position that we are in but we are seeing incremental growth on a monthly basis.
LUMKILE
13;26

So overall I think south Africa is in a far better position than it has been since last march when we instituted the lockdown. To really take off and deliver the growth that we’ve seen in the first quarterbut also the period of an exceptional recovery of our commodities. 13;50 as we have seen the prices have spiked and many of our firms in the mining sector are doing extremely well, which will see the multiply effects in other sectors going forward.

Slow, yet vital growth in some industries, according to Dr Lumkile Mondi, economic analyst at Wits University, some sectors of the economy are struggling to recover

LUMKILE
20;42 the most sectors that we’re still very concerned about is the construction sector eh, it’s been the pillar and economic indicator of an economic recovery so if we can get the construction sector in rebuilding the commtor infrastructure which has been destroyed as one of the sectors which is real, cause we know that there’s a big linkage between the construction sector as well as the manufacturing sector because in doing so you require steel. So those two are quite critical for the economic recovery
Preparations for the 2010 soccer world cup saw a roll out of large scale infrastructure projects and the economy was growing at around 5 percent annually.

Manufacturing economist Chifipa Mhango says whilst the president’s plan holds potential to grow the economy, its results will rely on implementation.
Chifipa 26;28 during the time of the soccer world cup projects of 2010, there was massive investment in terms infrastructure related to the world cup hosting, stadiums were being built, gautrain station was being build, we also had a good eh investment towards the energy sector especially looking at the kusile and medupi projects. That generated massive demand from the metals and engineering sector point of view to the point that the construction sector was growing between 15 and 25 percent, the manufacturing sector was groing almost 10 percent and during that period the economy overall was growing by 5 percent. The moment all those projects were completed we’ve seen almost a relaxed approach in terms of implementation of infrastructure investment and that has even taken a downward spiral in terms of how our economy has performed. So since 2008 we have not seen our economy performing above 5 percent. So it tells you the impact infrastructure investment, where there is a will to implement results in the south African economy

3 percent economic growth over the next decade may not be received as the perfect antidote for an economy that has been sluggish for years.

metadata.Summary: President Cyril Ramaphosa inherited a country facing serious economic woes, over the years he has devised various efforts to rekindle economic growth, his annual investment summits, various advisory groups etc. It is imperative especially after the devastation of the pandemic that the heavy lifting to fix the economy must start. One of the interventions outlined by the president in October last year was to 'unlock more than R1 trillion in infrastructure investment over the next four years'. In his budget speech, Finance Minister Tito Mboweni promised an injection of R700 billion into infrastructure development as a means to kick start the economy, both highlighting infrastructure as a cornerstone for the recovery of the economy. Another important focus of the economic reconstruction plan is to revitalise manufacturing in the country, in 1994 manufacturing accounted for 20 percent of the GDP and this has declined to 14 percent currently. Both these sectors are labour intensive and offer long term investment opportunities. However South Africa has a history of being lackadaisical when it comes to implementation of policy and creating plans on top of more plans. Due to the state of the economy, the implementation of this reconstruction plan is urgent for the country.
